title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202, 2023
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the policy problem of whether and how generative AI should be covered by the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA). The authors argue that generative AI systems may become gatekeepers in the same way as established digital platforms, creating risks of concentration, reduced contestability, and unfair dependence on a few dominant firms. Rather than presenting an empirical study, the paper develops a legal and regulatory argument for adapting the DMA to account for generative AI.

The proposed approach is to treat certain generative AI services as core platform services and, where appropriate, classify their developers as gatekeepers under the DMA. The paper discusses how generative AI can function as a platform through public chat interfaces and APIs, enabling downstream applications and reinforcing network effects. It also analyzes why leading providers such as OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta may gain durable advantages through computing power, early-mover advantage, data resources, and integrated systems.

The paper’s context is the EU regulatory environment, especially the DMA and its interaction with the AI Act and Digital Services Act. The authors conclude that existing DMA provisions could help curb unfair practices in generative AI, but only if the regulation is explicitly updated to cover these systems. They argue that such amendments would support openness, diversity, contestability, and fairness in the emerging generative AI market.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual legal/policy analysis rather than an empirical study. It contains no experimental, quasi-experimental, or observational outcome data and does not evaluate K-12 learning interventions.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact and no reported effect sizes. Its contribution is indirect and institutional, focused on AI market regulation rather than student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a normative/policy paper arguing that generative AI should be incorporated into the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) as a regulated core platform service. It does not report an empirical effect size, but it claims that doing so would improve contestability, fairness, and diversity in the generative AI market by constraining gatekeeper behavior and data/platform lock-in.
finding.measure: Policy and governance analysis of DMA applicability to generative AI services
